mcqs.question: A service has low, spiky traffic with long idle gaps between bursts. Which pricing model is likely cheaper?
options: Serverless, since it pays only for actual invocations rather than idle time between bursts
An always-on VM, since fixed costs are always lower regardless of traffic pattern
Both cost exactly the same regardless of traffic pattern
Neither pricing model can accommodate spiky traffic at all
mcqs.explanation: The VM bills for idle hours between bursts; serverless bills only for the invocations that actually occur, which is precisely why it wins for low, spiky volume.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't scale-to-zero help a workload with constant, steady traffic all day?
options: Scale-to-zero only works for workloads triggered by a queue
The workload never actually reaches zero traffic, so it never benefits from the 'pay nothing while idle' savings, and instead pays the per-invocation premium continuously
Steady workloads are technically incapable of running on a FaaS platform
Scale-to-zero requires a minimum of 24 hours of idle time before it activates
mcqs.explanation: Scale-to-zero's savings come entirely from idle periods; a workload with no idle periods gets none of that benefit and just pays per-invocation cost continuously.

mcqs.question: Why does FaaS lock-in go beyond typical cloud lock-in?
options: FaaS platforms require a multi-year contract before any code can be deployed
FaaS functions can only be written in one programming language per provider
Function code is often written against provider-specific event formats and triggers, so migrating means rewriting the integration layer, not just redeploying
There is no meaningful lock-in difference between FaaS and any other cloud service
mcqs.explanation: The lock-in is at the integration layer — event schemas, trigger wiring, provider-specific tooling — which a simple redeploy to another provider can't carry over.

mcqs.question: A team defaults to serverless for a workload with constant, round-the-clock traffic without checking the numbers. What's the likely outcome?
options: Cost savings identical to a spiky workload, since serverless pricing is traffic-pattern agnostic
No cost difference, since cloud providers price all workloads identically regardless of shape
The workload will fail to run at all under sustained load
A bill higher than a comparably-sized always-on VM, since the per-invocation premium is paid on effectively every request with no idle time to save on
mcqs.explanation: Serverless pricing is not traffic-pattern agnostic — its advantage depends entirely on idle time to save on, which a round-the-clock workload doesn't have, typically making it more expensive than a flat-rate VM at that volume.

mcqs.question: A function that hasn't changed and isn't under unusual load starts getting throttled. Investigation shows an unrelated function in the same account just spiked to its concurrency ceiling. What does this illustrate?
options: Serverless functions never share infrastructure or quotas with each other
Account-level concurrency and infrastructure are often shared across functions, so one workload's burst can indirectly starve another's capacity
The unrelated function's traffic has no possible effect on this one
This can only happen if both functions use the exact same trigger type
mcqs.explanation: Multi-tenant, shared account-level quotas mean a burst elsewhere in the same account can consume concurrency headroom that another function needed — a real cross-function contention risk that dedicated infrastructure doesn't have. It isn't limited to functions sharing a trigger type, and functions do share account-wide limits by default.
